overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Opening Mishna of Arakhin
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 2a–2b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Masechet Arakhin opens with the mishna: everyone takes vows of valuation, obligating themselves to donate the Torah-fixed sum for a person's age and sex (Leviticus 27:3–7), and everyone can themselves be valuated. It applies to priests, Levites, Israelites, women, and slaves; a tumtum and hermaphrodite may vow but cannot be valuated, since only a definite male or female qualifies; a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor can be valuated but cannot vow, since they lack presumed mental competence. The Gemara then works through the mishna clause by clause, asking what each 'everyone' (hakol) is meant to add beyond the obvious, and applies the identical technique to parallel mishnayot about sukka, lulav, tzitzit, tefillin, appearing in the Temple, and shofar — pausing along the way to debate whether an heir can place hands on, or substitute for, an inherited offering.

slides.title: 📜 The Opening Mishna: Four Categories
slides.subtitle: Two separate abilities — vowing and being valuated — do not always travel together
rows: The baseline group named in the mishna
'Only a definite male or a definite female are valuated'
'Because they lack the presumed mental competence' (da'at)

callout.label: Two more additions:
callout.text: 'Everyone valuates' adds a discriminating minor on the brink of adulthood (מוּפְלָא סָמוּךְ לְאִישׁ); 'everyone is valuated' adds a repulsive man or one afflicted with boils, who have no market value yet are still valuated.

slides.title: ⚖️ Can an Heir Place Hands or Effect Substitution?
slides.subtitle: The same 'his offering' vs. 'hamer yamir' dispute runs through Menachot and Temura

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: An heir places hands (סומך) on his father's offering, and an heir can effect substitution (מימר) for an offering he inherited.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: No — he expounds קׇרְבָּנוֹ, 'his offering' (Leviticus 3:2), meaning only one's own offering, not his father's. The initial stage of consecration (substitution) is derived from the final stage (placing hands): neither works for an heir.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: We read הָמֵר יָמִיר, the doubled 'if he shall substitute' (Leviticus 27:10), as including the heir — and we derive placing hands from substitution, the reverse direction.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: I use that same doubled 'hamer yamir' differently: to include a woman among those who may effect substitution, since the whole passage is otherwise phrased only in the masculine.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: We already learn that a woman may substitute from the extra letter in וְאִם הָמֵר יָמִיר, 'and if he shall substitute' — a letter Rabbi Yehuda does not expound at all.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Every extra letter or doubled verb in these verses is read by one side or the other as including either the heir or the woman — never both from the same word.

slides.title: 🔍 The Gemara's Method: What Does 'Everyone' Add?
slides.subtitle: A recurring question applied clause by clause to the mishna

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: 'everyone is valuated' (נֶעֱרָכִין) — what extra case does this add?
💭 Might think: a repulsive man or one with boils has no market value (no דָּמִים), so like anyone excluded from assessment, he should be excluded from valuation too

columns.label: If only 'according to your valuation'
columns.content: No monetary value → no valuation, since valuation is linked to assessment

columns.label: But the verse also says
columns.content: 'נְפָשֹׁת' — Persons — anyone with any amount of life is valuated, regardless of market price

nodes.content: ✅ Conclusion: the repulsive man and the one with boils ARE valuated, taught by the word 'nefashot' in the same verse

callout.label: Same technique elsewhere:
callout.text: The Gemara asks the identical 'what does this add?' question about a child less than a month old, learned from 'everyone is the object of a vow.'

slides.title: 🕎 Same Pattern, Five Mitzvot: What 'Everyone' Includes
slides.subtitle: The Gemara imports its method into other 'hakol' (everyone) statements across Shas

boxes.title: Sukka & Lulav
items: 'Everyone is obligated in sukka' — adds a minor who no longer needs his mother at night
'Everyone is obligated in lulav' — adds a minor who knows how to wave it

boxes.title: Tzitzit & Tefillin
items: 'Everyone is obligated in tzitzit' — adds a minor who knows how to wrap himself in a garment
'Everyone is obligated in tefillin' — adds a minor who knows to keep them in a state of cleanliness; his father buys him a pair

boxes.title: Shofar
items: 'Everyone is obligated to hear the shofar' — adds a minor who has reached the age of training (חִינּוּךְ)
One does not stop such a minor from sounding it on the Festival

callout.label: The pattern:
callout.text: Wherever a mishna says 'everyone,' the Gemara assumes it is teaching one specific, non-obvious inclusion — usually a minor at a particular stage of development.

slides.title: 🕊️ Who Must Appear in the Temple? The Half-Slave Case
slides.subtitle: 'Everyone is obligated in the mitzva of appearance' (Chagiga 2a) — reconciled with a famous Beit Hillel/Beit Shammai dispute

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: 'everyone is obligated in re'iya' adds one who is half-slave, half-freeman — but Ravina says such a person is actually exempt
2️⃣ Per Ravina, the addition must instead be one who was lame on day one of the Festival and healed on day two — obligated once healed

3️⃣ Background: Beit Shammai challenged Beit Hillel's ruling that a half-slave serves his master one day and himself the next — 'you fixed the master's share, but not his own: he can marry neither a maidservant nor a free woman'

4️⃣ Resolution: for the betterment of the world, the court forces the master to free him fully, and he writes a bill for half his value — Beit Hillel retracted to agree with Beit Shammai, and only then is he obligated to appear

callout.label: Two mishna versions:
callout.text: The 'included' and 'exempt' readings of the half-slave case map onto the earlier and later versions of the Beit Hillel/Beit Shammai mishna in Pesachim.

summary.principle: The mishna's broad word 'everyone' (hakol) is never read as mere emphasis; the Gemara treats each occurrence as hiding one precise, non-obvious halakhic addition, and applies the same interpretive method across arakhin, semikha, temura, and the mitzvot of sukka, lulav, tzitzit, tefillin, and shofar.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Mishna: everyone vows valuations and is valuated — except tumtum/androginos (not valuated) and deaf-mute/imbecile/minor (cannot vow)
🔍 Gemara's method: what does each 'everyone' add? → mufla samukh le'ish; repulsive man/boils via 'נפשות'; child under a month

columns.content: ⚖️ Heir & semikha/temura: R' Yehuda excludes him via 'קרבנו'; Rabbis include him via doubled 'הָמֵר יָמִיר'
🕎 Same pattern in sukka, lulav, tzitzit, tefillin, shofar — each adds one specific minor

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: no word in the mishna is superfluous — every 'everyone' hides a specific, derivable addition

quiz.q: According to the opening mishna, why can a tumtum and a hermaphrodite (androginos) vow to donate another's valuation but not themselves be valuated?
o: They lack the mental competence required to vow
Only a definite male or a definite female can be valuated
They are entirely exempt from Temple-related obligations
Their market value as slaves cannot be assessed
quiz.e: The mishna states they are not valuated 'since only a definite male or a definite female are valuated' — their sex is not definite.

quiz.q: Why are a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor the object of a vow of valuation but cannot themselves vow to donate someone's valuation?
o: They lack the presumed mental competence (da'at) to make a commitment
They have no monetary value on the open market
The Torah exempts them from all Temple gifts
They are considered legally dead for these purposes
quiz.e: The mishna gives the reason explicitly: 'because they lack the presumed mental competence,' so they cannot vow, though others can vow about them.

quiz.q: The Gemara includes a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils among those who are valuated, despite their having no market value. What word in the verse teaches this?
o: 'According to your valuation' (בְּעֶרְכְּךָ)
'Persons' (נְפָשֹׁת) — anyone with any amount of life
'A vow' (נֶדֶר)
'To the Lord' (לַה')
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that 'nefashot' teaches that anyone possessing any amount of life is subject to valuation, even without market value.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for ruling that an heir cannot place hands on, or effect substitution for, an offering he inherited?
o: He derives it from the doubled form 'hamer yamir'
He expounds 'his offering' (קׇרְבָּנוֹ) as excluding the father's offering, and derives the earlier stage (substitution) from the later stage (placing hands)
He holds that heirs are considered ritually impure
The Rabbis agree with this position
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda reads 'korbano' as 'his own offering, not his father's,' and reasons from the final stage of consecration (placing hands) to the initial stage (substitution) — an heir does neither.

quiz.q: How was the situation of one who is half-slave and half-freeman ultimately resolved, according to Beit Hillel's retracted position?
o: He remained a half-slave permanently
The court forces the master to free him fully, and he writes a bill of debt for half his value
He was sold to a non-Jew
He was declared entirely a slave
quiz.e: Beit Hillel retracted to agree with Beit Shammai: for the betterment of the world, the master is forced to free him, and the freed man commits by document to repay half his value.
